title: Verifying Whole Number Ratios (Law of Multiple Proportions)

notes: **Law of Multiple Proportions Verification:** When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other element are in ratios of small whole numbers. This law provides direct evidence for the atomic theory.

**Verification Method:** (1) Determine the mass of each element in each compound. (2) Fix the mass of one element. (3) Calculate the mass of the other element per fixed mass. (4) Find the ratio of these masses—it should be a simple whole number.
**Classic Example — Carbon Oxides:** In CO: 12g C combines with 16g O (ratio O/C = 1.33). In CO₂: 12g C combines with 32g O (ratio O/C = 2.67). The ratio of oxygen masses = 16:32 = 1:2.
**Nitrogen Oxides Verification:** NO (14g N : 16g O), NO₂ (14g N : 32g O), N₂O (28g N : 16g O). Normalized to 14g N: NO has 16g O, NO₂ has 32g O, N₂O has 8g O. Ratios: 8:16:32 = 1:2:4.

**Theoretical Basis:** This law arises because atoms combine in discrete, whole-number ratios. If element A combines with element B in compounds AB and AB₂, the mass of B per atom of A follows the ratio 1:2.
**Common Compounds to Verify:** (a) Copper oxides: Cu₂O (Cu:O = 4:1) vs CuO (Cu:O = 2:1), (b) Iron oxides: FeO vs Fe₂O₃ vs Fe₃O₄, (c) Sulfur oxides: SO₂ vs SO₃.
confusion: ❌ This law applies to all compounds. ✅ Only applies when TWO elements form MORE THAN ONE compound.
❌ The ratio must always be 1:1. ✅ The ratio can be any simple whole number (1:2, 2:3, 3:4, etc.).
❌ Experimental data will always give exact whole numbers. ✅ Real experimental data may have small errors; ratios should be close to whole numbers (e.g., 1.98 ≈ 2).
❌ This is the same as the Law of Definite Proportions. ✅ Definite proportions applies to ONE compound; multiple proportions applies to MULTIPLE compounds of the same elements.
practice: Calculate the mass ratio of oxygen in H₂O (1:8) and H₂O₂ (1:16) to verify the law.
Verify the Law of Multiple Proportions for SO₂ (S:O = 1:1) and SO₃ (S:O = 1:1.5).
Two oxides of nitrogen contain 36.4% and 69.6% oxygen respectively. Verify the law.
Show that Cu₂O and CuO obey the Law of Multiple Proportions using atomic masses Cu=63.5, O=16.
Given mass percentages for C₂H₆ and C₄H₁₀, verify the law for hydrogen-to-carbon ratios.
universalFacts: Whole number ratios are fundamental to chemical combination.
This verification supports the atomic theory of matter.
Experimental data consistently shows simple whole number ratios.
The law of multiple proportions is based on this observation.
This principle is used to determine empirical formulas.
examples: H₂O: H:O mass ratio = 1:8 (simple whole number ratio).
practiceQuestions: Verify whole number ratios for water and ammonia.
Calculate the empirical formula from percentage composition data.
Show that the Law of Multiple Proportions is based on whole number ratios.
formulas: Empirical formula: mole ratio of elements in simplest whole numbers
Mole ratio = (Mass of element / Atomic mass) for each element
Divide by smallest mole value to get whole number ratio
Molecular formula = (Empirical formula)_n where n = Molecular mass/Empirical mass
keyPoints: All compounds have whole number atom ratios.
Molecular formula may be multiple of empirical formula.
Whole number ratios support atomic theory.
enrichedContent.summary: The Law of Multiple Proportions states that when two elements form multiple compounds, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios. This law, formulated by Dalton in 1803, provides direct evidence for atomic theory by demonstrating that atoms combine in discrete, countable units.
specialNotes: This concept is essential for solving empirical formula problems.
NEB frequently asks to determine empirical formulas from data.
Round ratios to nearest whole numbers (multiply if needed).
importantStatements: Atoms combine in simple whole number ratios to form compounds.
The empirical formula represents the simplest whole number ratio of atoms in a compound.
Whole number ratios are evidence for the particulate nature of matter.
importantNotes: When calculating empirical formulas, divide mole ratios by the smallest value.
If ratios are not whole numbers, multiply by appropriate factor.
Common multipliers: ×2 for 0.5, ×3 for 0.33 or 0.67, ×4 for 0.25.
examShortTricks: Step 3: Divide by smallest mole value.
Step 4: Multiply to get whole numbers if needed.
examNotes: This law is a guaranteed NEB short-answer question—master verification procedures.
Be prepared to calculate mass ratios from percentage composition data.
Distinguish clearly from the Law of Definite Proportions in your answers.
Always show normalization to fixed mass in your calculations.
